title: Spelling rules (-s, -ing, -ed)
intro: Three endings do most of the work in English writing: **-s** for a third-person verb or a plural noun, **-ing** for progressive forms and gerunds, and **-ed** for a regular past. The base word usually stays exactly as it is, and the few changes that do happen follow a small number of patterns. These tables collect the patterns, with the exceptions that catch people out. Spellings here are British: *travelling*, *organise*, *practise* as a verb.

tables.caption: Adding -s to a verb after he, she or it
rows: Most verbs simply add -s.
read → reads · open → opens · arrive → arrives · cycle → cycles
The -s is never dropped, however long the subject is: *the boy next door **works** here*.
After -ch, -sh, -s, -x and -z, add -es.
teach → teaches · wash → washes · miss → misses · fix → fixes · buzz → buzzes
The ending becomes an extra syllable, which is why it is spelt with an e.
After -o, add -es.
go → goes · do → does · echo → echoes
Consonant + y becomes -ies.
study → studies · carry → carries · try → tries · apply → applies
Vowel + y keeps the y: play → plays · enjoy → enjoys · buy → buys.
Three verbs are irregular.
have → has · be → is · do → does
*does* and *goes* are spelt with -es but *says* is not: *she says*.

tables.caption: Making a noun plural
rows: Most nouns add -s.
book → books · student → students · essay → essays
After -ch, -sh, -s, -x and -z, add -es.
class → classes · watch → watches · box → boxes · bus → buses
Consonant + y becomes -ies.
city → cities · country → countries · family → families
Vowel + y keeps the y: day → days · key → keys · journey → journeys.
Many nouns ending in -f or -fe change to -ves.
leaf → leaves · knife → knives · shelf → shelves · wife → wives
But: roof → roofs · chief → chiefs · belief → beliefs · proof → proofs.
Nouns ending in -o are mixed.
potato → potatoes · tomato → tomatoes · hero → heroes
Shortened and borrowed words take -s: photo → photos · piano → pianos · kilo → kilos.
Some plurals change the word itself.
child → children · man → men · woman → women · foot → feet · tooth → teeth · person → people · mouse → mice
*people* is already plural, so it takes *are*, never *is*.
Some nouns do not change at all.
sheep · fish · series · species · aircraft · means
The verb still shows the number: *one series **is***, *two series **are***.
Academic words from Latin and Greek keep their own plurals.
analysis → analyses · crisis → crises · hypothesis → hypotheses · criterion → criteria · phenomenon → phenomena
*data* and *media* are already plural forms; in formal writing prefer *these data*, *the media are*.

tables.caption: Adding -ing
rows: Most verbs simply add -ing.
work → working · study → studying · carry → carrying
Unlike -s and -ed, the -ing ending never changes a final y.
Drop a silent final -e.
write → writing · make → making · take → taking · arrive → arriving
Keep the e in see → seeing, agree → agreeing and be → being.
One syllable ending in one vowel + one consonant: double the consonant.
stop → stopping · run → running · swim → swimming · plan → planning
Not after -w, -x or -y: show → showing · fix → fixing · play → playing.
Two syllables with the stress on the last one: double the consonant.
begin → beginning · prefer → preferring · permit → permitting · occur → occurring
Stress on the first syllable means no doubling: open → opening · visit → visiting · listen → listening.
In British spelling, a final -l after a single vowel doubles whatever the stress is.
travel → travelling · cancel → cancelling · label → labelling
American spelling keeps one l (*traveling*); stay with one system in a piece of work.
Final -ie becomes -y.
lie → lying · die → dying · tie → tying

tables.caption: Adding -ed to a regular verb
rows: Most verbs add -ed.
work → worked · watch → watched · open → opened
A verb ending in -e adds only -d.
arrive → arrived · hope → hoped · decide → decided
Consonant + y becomes -ied.
study → studied · carry → carried · apply → applied
Vowel + y keeps the y: play → played · enjoy → enjoyed · stay → stayed.
The doubling rules are the same as for -ing.
stop → stopped · plan → planned · prefer → preferred · travel → travelled
No doubling when the stress is on the first syllable: visit → visited · benefit → benefited.
Irregular verbs take no -ed at all.
teach → taught · write → wrote · build → built
Their forms are on the irregular verbs page; *teached* and *buyed* do not exist.

notes: Doubling only ever happens after **one** vowel letter. Two vowels together keep the single consonant: *rain → raining*, *read → reading*, *need → needed*, *sleep → sleeping*.
The -ed ending has three pronunciations — /t/ in *worked*, /d/ in *opened*, and an extra syllable /ɪd/ after t or d in *wanted* and *needed* — but the spelling is the same for all three.

British English prefers -ise in verbs such as *organise* and *realise*, and always spells *analyse* and *paralyse* with -yse. It also keeps *practice* for the noun and *practise* for the verb: *We need more **practice**, so we **practise** every Thursday.*
A spellchecker set to American English will quietly change *travelling*, *colour* and *organise*. Set the language of your document before you start writing.
